H.R. ___ 

120th Congress 

To provide pathways to prosperity by expanding economic opportunity, reducing regulatory barriers, promoting workforce development, supporting small businesses, reforming education, and empowering individuals and families to achieve self-reliance and break the cycle of poverty, and for other purposes.

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Dr. Báez (for himself and cosponsors) introduced the following bill, which was referred to the Committee on Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Small Business, and Financial Services. 

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE; TABLE OF CONTENTS.

(a) Short Title. This Act may be cited as the “Prosperity Through Opportunity Act.”

(b) Table of Contents. The table of contents for this Act is as follows:

Sec. 1. Short title; table of contents.
Sec. 2. Findings and purpose.
Sec. 3. Definitions.

TITLE I: WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT AND JOB TRAINING
TITLE II: SMALL BUSINESS AND ENTREPRENEURSHIP SUPPORT
TITLE III: EDUCATION REFORM AND SCHOOL CHOICE
TITLE IV: TAX INCENTIVES AND REGULATORY RELIEF
TITLE V: FAMILY AND COMMUNITY EMPOWERMENT
TITLE VI: ADMINISTRATION AND FUNDING

SECTION 2. FINDINGS AND PURPOSE.

(a) Findings. Congress finds the following:

(1) Persistent poverty in districts such as Texas’s 20th Congressional District stems not from a lack of government spending, but from barriers to opportunity, including failing public schools, excessive regulations, high taxes, family breakdown, and government dependency fostered by socialist-style policies.

(2) The American Dream is rooted in personal responsibility, free enterprise, faith, family, and hard work. Historical data show that education, stable two-parent families, full-time work, and avoidance of dependency are the strongest predictors of escaping poverty.

(3) Overregulation and bureaucratic red tape disproportionately harm low-income entrepreneurs and small businesses, which create the majority of new jobs.

(4) School choice and vocational training have proven effective in empowering families and preparing workers for high-demand careers.

(5) Targeted, pro-growth tax policies and regulatory relief, rather than expansive welfare programs, drive sustained economic mobility.

(b) Purpose. The purpose of this Act is to: 

(1) Expand economic opportunity by removing barriers to work, entrepreneurship, and upward mobility;

(2) Promote self-reliance, personal responsibility, and family stability;

(3) Reform education systems to prioritize skills, literacy, and workforce readiness over ideological indoctrination;

(4) Support small businesses and innovation in high-poverty communities;

(5) Reduce government dependency while protecting those truly in need; and

(6) Align federal policy with constitutional principles, limited government, and the values of faith-informed service to our communities.

SECTION 3. DEFINITIONS.

In this Act:

(1) Opportunity Zone. The term has the meaning given in section 1400Z-1 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

(2) Eligible Entity. Includes States, local governments, community colleges, trade schools, nonprofit organizations with proven track records of job placement (excluding those primarily engaged in advocacy), and faith-based organizations.

(3) [NAME]-Reliance Metric. A measurement developed by the Secretary of Labor, in consultation with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, that tracks exits from means-tested welfare programs, employment retention, wage growth, and family stability.

TITLE I: WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT AND JOB TRAINING

SEC. 101. EXPANSION OF WORKFORCE INNOVATION AND OPPORTUNITY ACT (WIOA) FLEXIBILITY.

(a) States shall receive block grants under WIOA with greater flexibility to prioritize apprenticeships, on-the-job training, and industry-recognized credentials over classroom-only programs.

(b) At least 60 percent of funds must demonstrate measurable outcomes in job placement and wage gains within 6 months.

SEC. 102. NATIONAL APPRENTICESHIP INCENTIVE PROGRAM.

(a) Establishes a tax credit of up to $5,000 per apprentice for employers who hire and retain individuals from high-poverty census tracts for registered apprenticeships in trades, manufacturing, healthcare, technology, and infrastructure.

(b) Prioritizes veterans, former foster youth, and individuals exiting the criminal justice system.

SEC. 103. VOCATIONAL EDUCATION GRANTS.

Authorizes $500,000,000 annually for competitive grants to community colleges and trade schools partnering with employers for short-term, high-return certification programs (e.g., welding, HVAC, nursing, coding, commercial driving).

SEC. 104. BAN ON USE OF FUNDS FOR IDEOLOGICAL TRAINING.

No funds under this title may support programs that include diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) mandates, gender ideology, or critical race theory content.

TITLE II: SMALL BUSINESS AND ENTREPRENEURSHIP SUPPORT

SEC. 201. MICRO-LOAN AND MENTORSHIP EXPANSION.

(a) Increases funding and eligibility for Small Business Administration microloans (up to $100,000) targeted at Opportunity Zones and high-poverty areas.

(b) Requires mentorship components through partnerships with SCORE, chambers of commerce, and faith-based organizations.

SEC. 202. REGULATORY RELIEF FOR SMALL BUSINESSES.

(a) Exempts businesses with fewer than 50 employees from certain federal regulations for the first 3 years of operation.

(b) Creates a “One-Stop Shop” federal portal for permitting and compliance assistance.

SEC. 203. NEW MARKETS TAX CREDIT EXTENSION AND EXPANSION.

Permanently extends and increases the New Markets Tax Credit with a focus on job-creating projects in distressed communities.

TITLE III: EDUCATION REFORM AND SCHOOL CHOICE

SEC. 301. FEDERAL SCHOOL CHOICE TAX CREDIT.

Creates a refundable tax credit for contributions to scholarship organizations that provide K-12 education savings accounts, enabling low-income families to choose private, public charter, homeschool, or vocational options.

SEC. 302. ACCOUNTABILITY FOR FAILING SCHOOLS.

(a) Withholds federal education funds from persistently failing Title I schools (as measured by NAEP and graduation rates) unless they implement proven reforms, including phonics-based reading, core skills curriculum, and removal of ideological content.

🏠 Re-Privatizing Fannie and Freddie: Don’t Introduce New Risks — Fix Housing Affordability First

Bill Ackman’s push to re-privatize Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — releasing them from conservatorship, restructuring or forgiving Treasury’s senior preferred stock, easing capital rules, and handing greater control to private shareholders — sounds like reform. It is not. In the current environment, it would privatize gains while leaving taxpayers with the downside, all without fixing what is driving the housing crisis.

Fannie and Freddie play a vital role as government-sponsored enterprises. They buy conforming loans (up to the current baseline limit of $832,750 in areas like Berks and Chester Counties in Pennsylvania), securitize them into mortgage-backed securities, and guarantee timely payment of principal and interest. This government-backed assurance, backed by real estate collateral, provides essential liquidity and keeps U.S. mortgage rates lower and more stable than a purely private market would deliver.

Since the 2008 bailout of roughly $191 billion, the GSEs have remitted well over $300 billion to taxpayers through dividends, sweeps, and guarantee fees (currently around 65 basis points). The system has been a net revenue generator while delivering systemic stability.

❌ The Real Source of the Housing Crisis

After spending time talking with real estate agents, home builders, and local housing professionals here in Chester County, one thing is clear: America’s housing affordability crisis is the direct result of two intersecting policy failures.

First, high conforming loan limits now support government-backed financing for homes approaching or exceeding $1 million. Second, excessive regulatory costs — zoning restrictions, lengthy permitting, environmental mandates, impact fees, and construction requirements — make it far more profitable for builders to focus on these larger, high-end homes instead of smaller, affordable starter or retirement units.

This combination severely distorts the market. New home construction has lagged long-term demand, remaining well below the levels needed to keep pace with population growth and household formation. As a direct consequence, most people in their twenties and thirties are effectively squeezed out of homeownership altogether. This is why first-time buyers now average around 40 years old in Pennsylvania.

💰 Leave the GSEs Alone — Fix Affordability First
Rather than rushing re-privatization and introducing new risks into an already unbalanced system that heavily favors million-dollar homes, we should leave Fannie and Freddie in their current conservatorship structure. The existing hybrid model provides proven liquidity and taxpayer returns. Changing it now would risk higher borrowing costs or weaker safeguards without addressing root causes.

🏠  Instead, policymakers should focus aggressively on the affordability crisis:

✅ Targeted lower rates for starter homes: The Federal Reserve should implement policies that deliver meaningfully lower interest rates specifically for smaller, entry-level homes (for example, those priced at or below the local median). This would help rebalance incentives away from luxury properties and make homeownership more accessible for younger families.

In fact, I have argued that 0% rate, fee-only loans up to the median home price (about $400K) that amortize over 10-15 years is what is needed to fix the market. The Federal Reserve could do this without new government consent to better achieve its dual mandates of low inflation and high employment, but Congress should be proactive in this regard. We should remember that the Federal Reserve provided near-zero rates for a long time, but the main beneficiaries were asset managers and wealthy investors — not average American families — since it was untargeted. But if the Federal Reserve targeted support for homes below median cost, it would be transformative and beneficial not just for young people but also for older folks and retirees. In other words, the Federal Reserve needs to use the same 0% QE tool it has in the past, but just in a targeted way.

✅ Attack regulatory barriers head-on: Slash zoning restrictions, streamline permitting, reduce unnecessary mandates, and lower construction-related costs at the local, state, and federal levels. These changes would encourage builders to construct the smaller starter and retirement homes that families actually need, increasing overall supply where it matters most.

Housing finance is inherently cyclical. Maintaining the current GSE backstop as a public good prevents localized problems from becoming national crises. But we cannot keep subsidizing million-dollar homes with taxpayer-backed guarantees while regulatory barriers block affordable construction for everyone else. Fix the supply distortions and rate misalignments first.

Only then will the system truly serve American families rather than high-end developers and investors. The housing market and younger Americans deserve solutions that expand opportunity, not experiments that shift more risk onto taxpayers. Keeping Fannie and Freddie stable while directly tackling regulatory barriers and delivering lower rates for starter homes is the practical way forward.
